catalog_locator: Connell 1994 sec. 3.3 'Tone systems', journal p. 10 and sec. 5, journal p. 12. Connell 1991 sec. 2.3.3.3 p. 55 with fn. 32, and fn. 34 p. 56.
catalog_quote: [p. 10] From a lexical standpoint, the tone systems found in the Lower Cross languages are relatively straightforward: in all languages of the group, there are two tones, high (H) and low (L), and contrastive downstep (D) which operates on H tones. ... Combinations of two tones on one syllable may occur, to give HL—i.e., a falling tone—or LH, a rising tone. Falling tones are common in some languages of the group, viz., Anaang (dialectally), Ebughu, Ibibio (dialectally), Ito, Itu Mbon Uso, Nkari, and Usaghade, where they are a result of tone spreading (H L H HL). ... From a phrasal perspective, the Lower Cross languages are of the classic terracing type; i.e., each instance of D within a phrase lowers the ceiling on H tones within that phrase, with the ceiling being reset at the beginning of each subsequent phrase. [p. 12] Tonal systems in the group appear to be further complicated through interaction with phrasal stress, but except for Faraclas (1984b) for Obolo, no investigation in this area has been done.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nkari is a two-tone (H, L) terraced-level language with contrastive downstep and H-spreading falling tones; the only thing said about stress is group-level: some phrasal stress interacting with tone is presumed but uninvestigated for every Lower Cross language except Obolo. No word-stress placement rule is stated for Nkari. Connell 1991 (group-level, Nkari not in that sample) adds that there is no true evidence for word stress in Efik/LC and calls LC 'a non-stress language', while allowing phrasal and compound-juncture stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the statement is group-level (all Lower Cross languages), with Nkari named explicitly only in the tone sentence.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone; stress mentioned only at phrase level ('phrasal stress'), not described. Data are from Connell's own 1990-91 Nkari fieldwork (1991: 7), published only as the appendix A comparative wordlist.
new_statements.identity_note: Nkari = Glottolog nkar1238 / ISO nkz, a language-level languoid under Ibuoro-ItuMbuso-Nkari (ibuo1243) < Ibuoroic < Central Lower Cross; spoken around Ini LGA, Akwa Ibom State, Nigeria. Connell 1994 treats it as a distinct Lower Cross language that 'could possibly be grouped together as a dialect cluster' with Itu Mbon Uso, Ibuoro and possibly Ito (p. 5); Blench 2020 indexes it as 'dialect of Ibibio. Probably a separate language: but no firm data (Bruce Connell)' and lists it among Ibibio clan dialects; Wikipedia/Ethnologue-derived lists make it a dialect of Ibuoro (ibr). The quoted statement is group-level (all Lower Cross), with Nkari named explicitly in the tone sentence; Connell's Nkari data (collected 1990-91, 1991: 7) appear only as the appendix A wordlist of the 1994 article. A sibling catalog note refers to 'nkar1239'; the correct Glottolog code is nkar1238.

sources.note: Nkari is in the sample (pp. 4-6, 9, 13; tone-marked Nkari row in the appendix A wordlist from p. 17). Sec. 3.3 p. 10: all LC languages have two tones H/L plus contrastive downstep; falling tones in Nkari (among others) arise from H-spreading. Sec. 5 p. 12: 'Tonal systems in the group appear to be further complicated through interaction with phrasal stress, but except for Faraclas (1984b) for Obolo, no investigation in this area has been done.' No word-stress rule for Nkari or any LC language.

sources.citation: Faraclas, Nicholas. 1984b. Tone and phrase stress: the extra high tone in Obolo. Journal of West African Languages 14(1): 3-17.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.note: This work describes Obolo (obol1243), Western dialects; Delta-Cross (Benue-Kwa), southeastern Nigeria. Nkari is never named or mentioned; the article is about Obolo only (the only language of the Lower Cross/Delta-Cross area it treats). Nothing in it bears on the Nkari catalog entry (tonal, lexical-tone, Connell 1994). The one Lower Cross study of 'phrasal stress' that Connell 1994: 12 and 1991: 55 cite; it defines what stress in the group is taken to mean (Obolo, not Nkari, so it would only frame the group-level statement).
